This article has great value as an analysis of where we stand, what is happening both to us and within our ranks (and what it means), and what we might expect next.

I have some extra thoughts (some in competition to the OP link, some not). I wrote these out kind of stream-of-conscious and hope they're not too confusing, but I just want to share to see if I'm alone on any of this.

A few things stood out to me about the assumptions I'm reading into the discussion points of this article:

  • The moderates are looking for outs: Going back to the earlier idea that 'moderates would rather be hated than ignored' I don't see any evidence that people are looking for a way to get out of GG. GG has won in the most substantive way, the 'hate-movement' stigma has all but nearly dissipated by my view and anyone who still says so is ignored. GG is seen now more as the mob-journo or the counter-culture hippies out there analyzing games and doing journalism organically through discussion. They've obviated the need for Kotaku by talking among themselves about the topics that barely get covered, and really kick into gear when they're covered wrong. To me that has value, and I would think it has value to more than just me. I literally get my news now in GG forums, because its more straightforward than finding it elsewhere. I think you'd call me a moderate because I barely participate in campaigns and am really just here to talk, but I feel zero pressure to leave or get off the sinking ship. If anything there feels like there's more of us all the time, the ship's getting bigger.

  • Definitions of success and failure: I get the impression that the definition of success for the points of this article is reforming the media (at large, not just games). I think it is hilarious that we're seen as a threat of that caliber. To me, we're just calling shit out to be shit on a very consistent and persistent basis. If that's all it takes to reform the media and we need to be divided and conquered to stop that, then they might give up now trying. People like me (a moderate by given definitions) will never stop doing that now that a platform exists for me to let shit be known. I now know where I can point out censorship, bias, double-think, media cronyism, and agenda ramming. And there are enough of us obsessed with the freedom to continue our open dialog that we left Reddit (that's a big show of dedication I think), and will move again if we have to. We know who we are and where to find each other. You can't diffuse that.

Now, if you set about to divide us into "those who chat" and "those who call advertisers and raise cane" I think you're going to have a bad time, because that isn't a line anyone can define with any certainty. I haven't seen (outside of organizing for interviews and panel debates) any emergence of credential checking and leadership bonafides. We just set up a campaign and motivate regular joes to jump in. I don't think we have such an exclusionary culture that we go behind and say "and if you aren't seen at the 'March for Misogyny' event, then you're out of the club." Any given campaign is going to have a mercurial group of activists. Me, I care deeply about stuff like the SF5 censorship. Damn straight I'm telling Capcom directly that I'm displeased with their pandering. And I doubt that there are many here who are nearly as motivated as I am to carry on over that. That's fine, there's other topics to cover and other campaigns to run.

Basically I think, given what I see of us here on this forum and some others. We're a group who share opinions, are unified around being ostracized and otherized for a DECADE or longer, are tired of having the issues we really care about be ignored or treated with disdain, and, thanks to their own gross over-play of their hand, have emerged together as a relatively cohesive and rebellious collective.

I have fun here, its the only place I go to talk on the internet anymore, none of the tactics they seem to outline here are going to affect me to make me leave, but then, maybe I've missed the point.
